toolu_016q1sy8v14UFhoGBE3CA6K6.content:
# The Name {#sec-the-name}

For about a month the script was called check.py.
That was what it did, and I was the only one who ever had to say it.

Then it was notes-check, which was more accurate and no better.

Then it was a directory with four files in it.
The notes had been a shoebox, then a spreadsheet, then a script, and each had outgrown the one before.
This was the first of them that needed a name.

It needed one because it was about to become a repository.
Every change I made to the script I made at night, and some of them I could not undo in the morning.
I write about version control for a living.
I had been meaning to take my own advice for about a month.

You can name a directory anything.
You can't call a repository "the thing for chapter four".

So I set aside an evening for names.
I opened a document, and by midnight it was a page long.

Most of them were puns.
Punctuation rewards a pun and shouldn't.
There were names about checking, names about notes, names about stops and pauses and things that hold sentences together.
Some were worse than puns.
One had the word *colon* in it, and I had not thought it through.

None of them was a name.
They were all jokes I would have to explain to whoever asked, and in the README, and to myself, every time I typed one.

I kept going, which is how two in the morning happens.

Around two I gave up on the page and opened a chat with Otto, meaning to ask something else entirely.
I typed "quirk".

Otto finished it as "quirework".

I looked at the word for a while.
It was not a pun.
It sounded like something that should already exist, and as far as I could find, it didn't.
I checked.

I liked it better than anything on the page.
I liked it better than anything I would have chosen, and I had spent the evening choosing.

I don't remember what I meant to ask.

I made the repository that night, before I could think better of it.
The first commit message was *Name it*.

I have written better commit messages since.
Not many.

In the morning I gave it a README, because a repository without one looks abandoned, and a version number, because a tool without one looks like a script.
The version number was zero point one, which promises nothing.
The README was a page long.
It was the shortest it would ever be.

Chapter four had not changed since the Sunday I wrote the script.
It had never been so consistent.

That week the script stopped being a script.
It had a name, a repository, a README and a version number.
It was a tool.

I was the only person who had ever used it.

# Nine Hundred Lines {#sec-nine-hundred-lines}

Red's emails kept saying "Checking in."
I kept answering them.

By the month the tool got its name, my answers had run out of things to say about chapter four.
Chapter four had not changed in weeks, and I could only describe a thing that had not changed so many ways.

So this time, I decided, I would send Red something.
Not an answer: an outline for chapter twelve.
An outline would show him the book was still moving, and show me where to.

I opened a new document and typed "Chapter twelve" at the top.
Then I sat with it.

The README was open in the next window.
It was usually open in the next window.

It had started a page long, the morning after the name.
Every evening since, the tool had learned to do something, and every new thing it did needed a paragraph.
Some of the paragraphs needed an example.
The examples needed a section to explain them.
There was a section on the configuration file, and a longer one on the second configuration file, which had been written to explain the first and no longer did.
There was a table of contents.
There was a list of known problems, in order of how much they embarrassed me.

It was the longest thing I had written that year.
It had headings, and headings look like progress.

The outline for chapter twelve was two words long, and one of them was a number.

I sent Red the README.
Above it I wrote three lines saying this was what I had been working on, for the book.
I did not say it was instead of the book.
I did not have to.
It was nine hundred lines.

I still think it was the best thing I wrote in those three years.
It was clear.
It was in order.
It said what the tool did, and the tool did it.
Nothing in it disagreed with anything else in it, which was more than I could say for anything else I had sent Red.

It was documentation, which is my job, which is the problem.

Red read all of it.
I know because months later, in an email about something else, he quoted line six hundred and twelve back to me.

That day he wrote back one line.

"Is there a chapter in here?"

I read the README again, top to bottom, the way he would have, looking for one.

There wasn't.
There was a section called Getting Started.

```
# Nine Hundred Lines {#sec-nine-hundred-lines}

Red's emails kept saying "Checking in."
I kept answering them.

By the month the tool got its name, my answers had run out of ways to describe a chapter that was not changing.

So this time, I decided, I would send Red something.
Not an answer: an outline for chapter twelve.
An outline would show him the book was still moving, and show me where to.

I opened a new document and typed "Chapter twelve" at the top.
Then I sat with it.

The README was open in the next window.
It was usually open in the next window.

It had started a page long, the morning after the name.
Every evening since, the tool had learned to do something, and every new thing it did needed a paragraph.
Some of the paragraphs needed an example.
The examples needed a section to explain them.
There was a section on the configuration file, and a longer one on the second configuration file, which had been written to explain the first and no longer did.
There was a table of contents.
There was a list of known problems, in order of how much they embarrassed me.

It was the longest thing I had written that year.
It had headings, and headings look like progress.

The outline for chapter twelve was two words long, and one of them was a number.

I sent Red the README.
Above it I wrote three lines saying this was what I had been working on, for the book.
I did not say it was instead of the book.
I did not have to.
It was nine hundred lines.

I still think it was the best thing I wrote in those three years.
It was clear.
It was in order.
It said what the tool did, and the tool did it.
Nothing in it disagreed with anything else in it.
I could not say that about anything else I had ever sent Red.

It was documentation, which is my job, which is the problem.

It was documentation, which is my job, which is the problem.
```

Wait, that last block repeats a line by mistake in this message only; the file has it once and continues:

```
Red read all of it.
I know because months later, in an email about something else, he quoted line six hundred and twelve back to me.

That day he wrote back one line.

"Is there a chapter in here?"

I read the README again, top to bottom, the way he would have, looking for one.

There wasn't.
There was a section called Getting Started.
```

**Length:** about 400 words, so part two runs short on purpose, as you said is fine. Hedda stays out of this chapter, because her third answer belongs to The Demo. The chapter ends on Getting Started and doesn't say what you did next.

**Details I made up, for you to keep or cut:**
- The outline being two words long, "and one of them was a number."
- The README sitting in the next window, and its parts: the section on the second configuration file that "no longer did" explain the first, the table of contents, and the list of known problems ranked by embarrassment.
- The three-line note above the README, and "I did not say it was instead of the book."
- "Nothing in it disagreed with anything else in it. I could not say that about anything else I had ever sent Red." This is the line closest to stating the book's thesis. If it reads as explaining, cut it.

**Lines that call back to earlier chapters:**
- "Headings look like progress" echoes chapter one's "length can be mistaken for progress."
- "Page long, the morning after the name" picks up where The Name leaves the README.

I didn't say what line six hundred and twelve said. If you remember, it might be worth a sentence.

**Files I changed besides the chapter:**
- **Spec `#people-who-ask`:** Red's paragraph now holds the outline you meant to send, why you sent the README instead, "which is my job, which is the problem", line six hundred and twelve, and Getting Started. `quirework text wrap` rewrapped only that paragraph.
- **Trail:** I added a `sharpen` breadcrumb on `people-who-ask`. Like the one for The Name, it reads from this session's live transcript and only holds once you capture the session with `quirework provenance ingest claude`.
- **Sidecar:** I removed the todo and added two guidance notes: Hedda stays out of this chapter, and it ends on Getting Started. The `people-who-ask` binding still holds.

Say the word and I'll commit it.
